summary: This work demonstrates that noise at frequencies matching the dressed-state energy splitting $2g$ (set by inter-qubit coupling) induces a distinct relaxation channel in coupled superconducting qubits during two-qubit gates, with gate errors scaling as $\epsilon_\mathrm{avg} = \frac{1}{5}\Gamma_g \tau$ where $\Gamma_g = \frac{1}{2}S_\Delta(2g)$. The mechanism, validated experimentally on tunable transmon qubits with engineered noise spectra from 5–20 MHz, extends the concept of $T_{1\rho}$ relaxation to interacting systems and applies universally to dual-rail and singlet-triplet encodings.
motivation: Realistic qubit environments exhibit structured, frequency-dependent noise spectra rather than white or quasi-static noise; understanding how this frequency-selective noise impacts gate performance is essential for error budgeting and mitigation in quantum processors.
method: Theoretical analysis using Bloch–Redfield theory combined with experimental verification: injected classical Gaussian noise (filtered to 5–20 MHz passband) was applied to transmon qubits during spin-locking and two-qubit gate operations; dressed-state relaxation rates were measured independently and related to gate fidelity via cross-entropy benchmarking.
result: Measured dressed-state relaxation rates $\Gamma_g$ and single-qubit $T_{1\rho}$ rates agree when $2g = \Omega/2\pi = 15$ MHz, with slopes $\partial\Gamma_g/\partial P_\mathrm{out} = 1.13\,(\mathrm{mW}\cdot\mu\mathrm{s})^{-1}$; fSim gate errors scale linearly with $P_\mathrm{out}$ and interaction time $\tau = 48$ ns in excellent agreement with theory, confirming that suppressing noise near $2g$ is critical for high-fidelity entangling gates.
